When you "have it out with someone," it means you confront that person directly and openly about a problem, conflict, or grievance — usually in a heated, blunt, and emotionally charged way — with the goal of settling the matter once and for all.

Think of it this way: imagine you have been quietly tolerating something that bothers you — maybe a friend keeps breaking promises, a coworker keeps taking credit for your work, or a family member keeps making hurtful comments. Instead of staying silent, you finally decide: "Enough. I am going to face this person and say everything that needs to be said." That bold, direct confrontation is what "having it out" means.

The word "out" is the key here. It means bringing everything that was hidden, swallowed, or kept inside — out into the open. Nothing left unsaid. No more avoiding the issue.

PartWhat It Refers To
"Have"To engage in, to carry out
"It"The unresolved problem, conflict, or grievance between two people
"Out"Into the open; completely; without holding back
"With someone"The specific person you are confronting

"Have" means to engage in or carry out something. "It" refers to the unresolved conflict or grievance sitting between you and the other person. "Out" means bringing it fully into the open — nothing held back. "With someone" points to the specific person you are addressing. Together, the phrase means: to bring a buried conflict fully into the open with the person involved, and deal with it head-on.

This idiom carries a strong emotional weight. It is not a calm, polite chat. It is not a gentle nudge. When someone "has it out" with another person, the conversation is usually:

  • Frank and blunt — people say exactly what they mean
  • Emotionally charged — raised voices, frustration, and tension are common
  • Exhaustive — everything that has been building up finally comes out
  • Confrontational — someone is being directly faced about their behaviour or actions

However — and this is important — the intention behind the idiom is often constructive, not purely destructive. The idea is to clear the air, not just to fight. Think of it like a pressure cooker: the steam (tension) has been building, and "having it out" releases it all at once so the situation can finally be resolved.

This phrase has been used in English since at least the 19th century. The idea is rooted in an old sense of the word "out" meaning to exhaust something completely or to fight it to a finish. In old usage, you could "fight it out" (settle a fight until one side wins) or "argue it out" (argue until the matter is resolved). "Have it out" follows the same logic — you are dealing with the problem until it is fully exhausted and settled. The "it" always refers to the unresolved issue hanging between two people.
Sentence Examples (From Simple to More Complex)

Simple situations:

  • "I finally had it out with my roommate about the dirty dishes. We talked for an hour, but at least everything is clear now."
  • "He's been making rude jokes at my expense for months. I'm going to have it out with him tomorrow."

Workplace situations:

  • "She decided to have it out with her manager about being passed over for the promotion."
  • "After weeks of unfair treatment, the employees had it out with the supervisor during the team meeting."

Family or relationship situations:

  • "The two brothers had avoided each other for years, but at their mother's birthday, they finally had it out with each other."
  • "I love my best friend, but I need to have it out with her about constantly cancelling plans at the last minute."

With outcome mentioned:

  • "They had it out with each other, and although it was painful, they came out of it with a much better understanding."
  • "He had it out with his neighbour, but things only got worse afterwards."

Notice from the last two examples: having it out does not guarantee a good ending. It can lead to resolution and a better relationship, or it can make things worse. The idiom simply describes the act of the confrontation, not its outcome.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The structure is always:

have it out + with + [person]

The word "it" is fixed. You cannot say "have the problem out" or "have the argument out." It is always simply "it." The "it" is understood by everyone in context to mean the unresolved matter between the two people.

Here is how it looks across different tenses:

  • Present: "I need to have it out with him."
  • Future: "She is going to have it out with her sister tonight."
  • Past: "They had it out with each other last week."
  • Present perfect: "We have finally had it out, and I feel much better."

You can also use "each other" instead of a specific person when both sides are confronting one another mutually:

  • "The two rivals finally had it out with each other at the conference."

To understand an idiom deeply, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean a casual conversation. "Let's have it out with John over coffee" would sound odd because the phrase implies high emotion, not a relaxed chat.
  • It does not mean physical violence. It is strictly about verbal confrontation.
  • It does not mean gossip or talking about someone behind their back. You have it out with someone — meaning directly to their face.
  • It does not always mean the problem gets solved. It just means the confrontation happened.

• "Clear the air with someone" — This is softer and more mutual. It suggests a calm, two-sided conversation to remove tension. Less heated than "have it out."
  • "Confront someone" — Similar, but "confront" focuses on the act of facing them, while "have it out" emphasises the complete, exhaustive nature of the discussion.
  • "Hash it out" — This means to work through a problem together, often through discussion and negotiation. It is more collaborative and less emotionally charged than "have it out."
  • "Give someone a piece of your mind" — This is one-sided; you are expressing your anger or frustration at someone. "Have it out" implies a two-sided exchange where both people speak.
  • "Settle the score" — This has a darker, more revenge-like tone. "Have it out" is about confronting a conflict, not necessarily about revenge.
A Helpful Way to Remember It

Picture two people who have been avoiding an awkward, painful topic for a long time. The tension is like a knot between them. One day, one of them says: "We need to talk — really talk." They sit down, voices rise, feelings come flooding out, old grievances surface, hard truths are spoken. By the end, that knot — for better or for worse — has been untied. That is what "having it out" looks like.

The phrase essentially means: to drag a conflict out from the shadows and deal with it fully, directly, and honestly with the person involved — no more hiding, no more hinting, no more tolerating in silence.
